title: Getting Involved in Your Community
objectives: Describe ways to participate in neighbourhood and community life as a newcomer
Understand how community meetings, neighbourhood associations, and volunteer opportunities work
Use reported speech to share what others have said about community events and resources
Write a message to a neighbour or community group about a local issue

reading_passage.title: More Than a Neighbour: Becoming Part of the Community
reading_passage.text:
For many newcomers, the first months in a new country are spent focusing on survival — finding work, learning the transit system, managing bills, and getting children into school. Building a social life and becoming part of the neighbourhood often comes later. But community advocates say that engaging early, even in small ways, can significantly reduce the isolation many immigrants experience.

Portland is organised into more than ninety neighbourhood coalitions, each of which holds regular public meetings where residents can raise concerns, hear about local projects, and vote on how neighbourhood improvement funds are spent. These meetings are open to all residents regardless of immigration status, and translation services are sometimes available. Attending even once gives newcomers a sense of how decisions are made at the local level.

Volunteer work is another effective way to build connections. Organisations such as Catholic Charities, Oregon Food Bank, and the Muslim Community Center of Portland regularly recruit volunteers for food distribution, tutoring, and event support. Volunteer coordinators often say that many of their most committed volunteers are newcomers who want to give back to the community that supported them on arrival.

Small acts also matter. Introducing yourself to a neighbour, attending a free event at the library, or joining a community garden are all ways of becoming a familiar face. Somali community members in Portland have formed several informal networks — WhatsApp groups, Friday gatherings, and community dinners — that help both recently arrived and longer-settled families stay connected and share practical information.
reading_passage.source: Adapted from Portland Bureau of Planning and Sustainability community engagement resources and IRCO community integration materials, 2023

glossary.meaning: a group of people or organisations that come together to work toward a shared goal
the feeling of being disconnected from people around you, with few social connections
to find and invite new people to join an organisation or take part in an activity
dedicated and reliable; willing to give time and effort to something over a long period
an unofficial group of people who share information and support each other without a formal structure

comprehension.question: According to the passage, what can residents do at Portland neighbourhood coalition meetings?
comprehension.answer: They can raise concerns, hear about local projects, and vote on how neighbourhood improvement funds are spent.

comprehension.question: What does the author imply when they say volunteer coordinators describe newcomers as 'among their most committed volunteers'?
comprehension.answer: The author implies that newcomers who have received help on arrival often feel a strong motivation to give back — suggesting that volunteering benefits both the organisation and the newcomer's sense of purpose and belonging.

comprehension.question: What does 'isolation' mean in the first paragraph?
comprehension.answer: The feeling of being disconnected from other people and the community — having few social connections, which many newcomers experience in their first months.

comprehension.question: Why does the author mention Somali WhatsApp groups and community dinners at the end of the passage?
comprehension.answer: To show that community connection does not have to be formal — informal networks within one's own cultural community are also a meaningful and practical way to stay connected and reduce isolation.

language_focus.title: Reported Speech (Saying What Someone Else Said)
language_focus.explanation: When we report what someone else said, we use reported speech. The reporting verb (said, told, mentioned, explained, asked) introduces the report, and the tense in the reported clause usually shifts back one step: present → past, will → would, can → could. The pronoun and time references also change to match the new context.

examples.sentence: The volunteer coordinator said that many newcomers were among their most committed volunteers.
examples.note: 'Are' in the original becomes 'were' in reported speech. 'Said that' introduces the reported clause.

examples.sentence: She told me that the neighbourhood meeting would be held on Thursday evening.
examples.note: 'Will be held' in direct speech becomes 'would be held' in reported speech. 'Told me that' requires an object.

practice.sentence: Change to reported speech: 'The coordinator said: "Translation is available at the meetings."'
practice.answer: The coordinator said that translation was available at the meetings. (Present 'is' shifts to past 'was.')

practice.sentence: Change to reported speech: 'My neighbour told me: "There is a free community dinner on Friday."'
practice.answer: My neighbour told me that there was a free community dinner on Friday. ('Is' becomes 'was'; 'on Friday' stays as a reference point.)

practice.sentence: Which is correctly reported? Direct speech: 'She said: "I can volunteer on weekends."' A) She said she can volunteer on weekends. B) She said she could volunteer on weekends.
practice.answer: B) 'Can' shifts to 'could' in reported speech — 'she said she could volunteer on weekends' is the correct form.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: A group of people or organisations united to work toward a shared goal, often at a community or political level
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Portland is organised into more than ninety neighbourhood coalitions, each of which holds regular public meetings where residents can raise concerns.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: The feeling of being alone and cut off from meaningful contact with the community around you
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Community advocates say that engaging early, even in small ways, can significantly reduce the isolation many immigrants experience.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: To actively invite and bring new people into an organisation or activity
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Organisations such as Oregon Food Bank regularly recruit volunteers for food distribution, tutoring, and event support.

speaking_task.context: A newly arrived Somali family has asked you how to get more involved in the community. They have been in Portland for three months and feel isolated. They have two teenage children.
speaking_task.prompt: Share at least three ways the family can get involved in the community. Report advice you have heard from others (using reported speech) and include personal recommendations. Explain why each option would be good for their specific situation.
useful_language: My case worker told me that neighbourhood coalition meetings are open to everyone, even if you don't have a green card yet.
A friend said that Oregon Food Bank is always looking for volunteers, and it's a good way to meet people.
I've heard that the library has a free conversation group — someone told me it helped them improve their English and make friends.
speaking_task.model_answer: I know how isolating those first months can feel. Let me share three things that have helped people in similar situations. First, my case worker told me that every Portland neighbourhood has a coalition that holds public meetings — she said anyone can attend regardless of status. For the teenagers, a volunteer coordinator at the Oregon Food Bank told me they welcome young volunteers on weekends. And a friend of mine said the library on Division Street runs a free conversation group on Tuesday mornings — she told me it really helped her English and that she made several friends there. I'd start with the library — it's the most relaxed option.

writing_workshop.model_text:
Dear Neighbours,

My name is Faadumo and I have been living in apartment 7 for the past three months. I recently heard about the neighbourhood association meeting next week and I would like to attend. A friend told me that residents can raise concerns about local issues at these meetings.

I have noticed that the streetlight outside our building has not been working for several weeks. I would like to report this at the meeting and find out who is responsible for repairs.

Could someone let me know the exact time and room number for the meeting? I look forward to meeting more of my neighbours.

Sincerely,
Faadumo Osman, Apartment 7
writing_workshop.model_analysis: Notice how the writer introduces herself, uses reported speech naturally ('A friend told me that...'), raises a specific community issue, and ends with a polite request. The tone is warm but professional — appropriate for a first message to a community group.
writing_workshop.task: Write a message to your neighbourhood association or a community group. Introduce yourself, mention something you heard about the group (using reported speech), describe a local issue or a way you would like to get involved, and ask a question or make a request.
success_criteria: Introduce yourself and provide a brief context in the opening
Use reported speech at least once (e.g., 'I heard that...,' 'Someone told me that...')
End with a clear question or polite request for further information

quiz.question: According to the passage, who can attend Portland neighbourhood coalition meetings?
options: Only homeowners and long-term residents
Only US citizens and permanent residents
All residents regardless of immigration status
Only people who have registered in advance
quiz.explanation: The passage states: 'These meetings are open to all residents regardless of immigration status, and translation services are sometimes available.'

quiz.question: Why does the passage describe some newcomers as 'committed' volunteers?
options: Because they are paid more than other volunteers
Because they have received support on arrival and want to give back
Because they have more free time than long-term residents
Because organisations require more hours from newcomers
quiz.explanation: The passage says volunteer coordinators note that 'many of their most committed volunteers are newcomers who want to give back to the community that supported them on arrival.'

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses reported speech?
options: She said the meeting is on Thursday.
She said the meeting was on Thursday.
She said that the meeting will be on Thursday.
She said that the meeting is been on Thursday.
quiz.explanation: In reported speech, the present tense shifts to past — 'is' becomes 'was.' 'She said the meeting was on Thursday' is the correct reported speech form.

quiz.question: What does the passage say Somali community members in Portland have created to stay connected?
options: A formal non-profit organisation registered with the city
WhatsApp groups, Friday gatherings, and community dinners
A community centre funded by the Portland Bureau of Housing
A neighbourhood coalition in Southeast Portland
quiz.explanation: The passage mentions: 'Somali community members in Portland have formed several informal networks — WhatsApp groups, Friday gatherings, and community dinners.'

quiz.question: What is a 'coalition'?
options: A single person
A group of people or organisations united to work toward a shared goal
A rent payment
A library branch
quiz.explanation: A coalition is a group of people or organisations united to work toward a common goal — like Portland's neighbourhood coalitions.

quiz.question: According to the passage, what do advocates say about engaging with the community early?
options: It is a waste of time
It can significantly reduce the isolation many immigrants experience
It should wait several years
It costs a lot of money
quiz.explanation: The passage says 'engaging early, even in small ways, can significantly reduce the isolation many immigrants experience.'

quiz.question: Choose the correct reported speech: She said, 'I am busy.'
options: She said she is busy.
She said she was busy.
She said I am busy.
She say she busy.
quiz.explanation: In reported speech, the present ('am') usually shifts back to the past ('was'): 'She said she was busy.'

quiz.question: What does 'recruit' mean?
options: To leave a group
To actively invite and bring new people into an organisation
To pay a membership fee
To hold a meeting
quiz.explanation: To recruit means to actively invite and bring new people into an organisation or group.

listening_exercises.transcript: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the neighborhood association meeting. Tonight we have three topics: the new crosswalk on Elm Street, the summer festival in June, and volunteers for the community garden. If you'd like to speak, please raise your hand and say your name first. Coffee and cookies are in the back. Let's begin with the crosswalk.
listening_exercises.question: What should you do if you want to speak at the meeting?
options: Stand at the back
Raise your hand and say your name
Write a letter first
Wait until June

listening_exercises.transcript: Volunteering is a great way to meet neighbors and practice English at the same time. Schools often need helpers for events, food banks need people to sort donations, and parks need volunteers for clean-up days. You don't need perfect English — you just need to show up and help. Many people find friends, and even jobs, through volunteering.
listening_exercises.question: What does the speaker say you need to volunteer?
options: Perfect English
A special license
To show up and help
Experience
